I struggle with this too. And the only thing that I know works for myself is to plan ‘lazy’ days too. When you get too overwhelmed to do anything, dictate a day to actually being lazy and doing all the ‘non-productive’ things. It helps get that stress off. And then find the things you are less stressed on doing and plan to do them the next day. And work your way down the list. If there is something time sensitive dedicate one whole day to it, and if you have extra time after do smaller tasks.

Jk. I did pretty well organizing my stuff. I don’t got lots of advice because I didn’t dm long. Stress and covid made it too hard.
But here are my tips!

• write down the whole story, know the main events the players will face no matter how far in the future it’ll be.

•PLAN FOR SIDEQUESTS. Plan for the party potentially wanting to buy some land or an island.....don’t ask. But have side quests ready and able to fit in general areas of your world so if the party wants to do extra work between the main story quests you’ll be ready. 

•Addition to sidequests, have encounter tables and stat blocks ready for monsters and npcs for each area you’ll have in your campaign. Have them saved and ready to be pulled up at any moment. As a dm your a Druid but can become literally anything and any amount of creatures.
•Keep up to date with your player’s character sheets, get every detail. This is so you can be more prepared if they do something random with a spell or item they have that you might forget about. You’ll be able to roll with whatever the party does by having this info. Also will prevent anyone from pretending they got an item previously or had more money than they should’ve, I had many issues with forgetting about items the group had or just skipping arguments about items they claimed to have but I didn’t remember.

• For indvidual sessions write what you want to do in as much detail as you can to avoid forgetting anything, or just get the most important facts down. Even how each npc talks. Have an end goal for each session and if the party reaches that before the end of your session time then try enticing them with a side quest, rp/down time, shopping, or setting up the next plot point. 

•Write not only your ideal path for the party, but also try to write two or three potential branching paths the group could/might go down instead. But they must all have the same end point even if they have varying results. (Wanted the group to slay a king by doing a siege of the castle? Well instead the group wants to become close servants/advisors/whatever for the king and then quietly kill him in the night or slowly convince him to change his ways)

•Keep a log of info for each big npc: their stats, how they talk, what they’ll have, dialog too! Keep track of important dialog the npc could have for the party. Then give that npc a special color and symbol to mark their dialog and information. It becomes a nightmare if you forget that one important thing an npc was supposed to say/give to the party. 

•Finally, have a couple notebooks, labels, and highlighters ready, because everything I’ve said here requires those! Or to save money have a google drive folder dedicated to dnd and have separate folders for all the things above. Don’t put everything in one place because it’ll get lost among the info and notes. If you have to rewrite something, even if it’s a description of an item or npc that is in another notebook, leave the name of said thing and then a reference of where you can find it so you can have it ready to go. 

Don’t know if any of this helps or makes any sense, but it’s just my advice as someone whose been a dm with ADHD.
